doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: Writing, criticism and the jazz business
title: Making a living in jazz and preparing students
summary: Thomas says there are too few venues for the number of jazz graduates, and that students need well-rounded skills; he prefers the term jazz journalist to critic.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Right. I’ve often wondered, is it harder to make a living as a jazz musician or as a jazz journalist?

It’s relative. I would say it’s — these days it probably is hard to be a jazz musician because you have situations where you have so many musicians and so relatively few places to play, and particularly places that pay anything decent. I mean there was a time I hear about or read about, or I’ve read about and have been told about, because I’ve done a bunch of interviews myself for the National Jazz Museum of Harlem, their “Harlem Speaks” series, I co-produced that and did dozens of interviews. And you hear these accounts of clubs here and there in various cities, and how it was just a part of the whole scene. That changed in the 60s, 70s, and 80s. You have these ups and downs. You have these waves of course, of where jazz is more or less recognized and appreciated, but it’s rough for jazz musicians. Especially when you have so many jazz musicians, young jazz musicians, coming out of jazz programs. There’s more jazz musicians coming out of jazz programs than there are bands — well not bands — but I’ll say places, venues, for them to work I think. So that’s problematic.

Yeah. Winard Harper was saying the same thing. And it’s rather ironic that in one sense jazz has become much more popular and healthy in academia, but that curve going up is sort of matched by the curve going down.

Right, right. So I think the key would be to make sure that those students are prepared. Say listen, it’s great to be an instrumentalist and to know how to do that and to be as good as you can with that, but that in the current marketplace you need to definitely be well- rounded, which a liberal arts education is supposed to give you, and to have some specific skill sets that you can apply in other areas other than music, but even in music there are any number of things that are needed. Certainly fundamentally these people will hopefully be jazz fans all of their life and bring others into the music, even if it’s just their own children. But there is other things that’s needed. You know when you talk about an industry you have different parts of that industry and how people fit. You know musicians often disparage critics. I consider myself a jazz writer though, and I’m a jazz critic to a certain extent, I think in a neutral to a positive sense, but because critics are so bedeviled by a negative connotation I think I lean toward jazz journalist.
